summary: Specifies a fast mechanism to protect pseudowires over IP/MPLS tunnels against egress failures, using multihomed CE, redundant pseudowires and upstream label assignment.

eli5.summary: A spare path ready beforehand so traffic switches fast if the exit fails.

questions: what is egress protection for pseudowires
what is a context identifier in mpls
what is a point of local repair
subtitle: Lets a router just before a failed pseudowire endpoint reroute traffic to a backup in tens of milliseconds.

tldr.problem: Pseudowires had fast protection for ingress failures and transit failures, but nothing equivalent for a failed egress attachment circuit, egress PE or switching PE. Recovery had to wait for global repair or control-plane convergence.
tldr.mechanism: The router just upstream of the failure (the point of local repair) reroutes traffic through a pre-built bypass tunnel to a protector. The protector already holds the failed PE's pseudowire labels, learned over LDP, and forwards the traffic to the backup path.
tldr.outcome: Traffic can be restored in the order of tens of milliseconds while global repair and convergence finish the job. The mechanism is meant to complement those, not replace them.

facts.label: Repair speed
facts.value: In the order of tens of milliseconds

facts.label: Context identifier
facts.value: An IPv4 or IPv6 address per {primary PE, protector}

today: RFC 8104 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It applies to LDP-signaled pseudowires and is intended to complement global repair and control-plane convergence.

sections.title: The Egress Protection Gap
sections.content:
A pseudowire (PW) carries an emulated Layer 2 service between two provider edge routers (PEs) across a packet network, with each PE binding the PW to an attachment circuit (AC) toward the customer. A multi-segment PW (MS-PW) is stitched through switching PEs (S-PEs).

To protect a PW service, every link and node on the path needs protection. The RFC notes that ingress AC and ingress PE failures can be handled by a multihomed customer edge (CE) with redundant ACs, and transit router failures by RSVP fast reroute (RFC 4090) or IP/LDP fast reroute (RFC 5286, RFC 5714). There was no equivalent for egress AC failure, egress PE failure or S-PE failure. Those relied on global repair or control-plane convergence, which are relatively slow.

RFC 8104 fills that gap for LDP-signaled PWs, in networks with redundant PWs and multihomed CEs. It builds on MPLS upstream label assignment and context-specific label switching (RFC 5331).
sections.eli5: Most breaks along a delivery route already had a quick fix. The very last stop did not, so this RFC adds one.

sections.title: Reference Models
sections.content:
The reference topology has a CE at each end, each multihomed to two PEs. In the single-segment case, PW1 runs between PE1 and PE2 and PW2 between PE3 and PE4. For traffic from CE1 to CE2 over PW1, PE2 is the primary egress PE, PE2-CE2 the primary egress AC, and PE4 and PE4-CE2 the backup egress PE and AC. The multi-segment case adds S-PEs, with PW1 switched at SPE1 and PW2 at SPE2.

A CE may run its ACs in active-standby mode (traffic only on the active AC until it detects a failure) or active-active mode (traffic load-balanced over both). The RFC says a dual-homed CE should not assume which AC a packet from the remote CE will arrive on, because fast protection can move traffic to the standby path.

Protection is described per active path and per direction. A failure in the reverse direction counts as an ingress failure, which is out of scope. The later switch of the CE to the backup path is global repair and also out of scope; this mechanism only reduces loss before that happens.
sections.eli5: There are two roads from one house to another, a main road and a spare. Each direction of travel is treated on its own.

sections.title: Local Repair with a Bypass Tunnel
sections.content:
The router upstream of a failure is the point of local repair (PLR). It MUST detect failures quickly, using physical-layer detection, BFD (RFC 5880), Seamless BFD (RFC 7880) or similar. In advance, it MUST pre-establish a bypass tunnel to a protector and pre-install the bypass route in the data plane. The protector is either a backup PE or a router that forwards on to one.

The PLR differs by case. For egress AC failure, it is the primary PE and the protector is the backup PE. For egress PE or S-PE failure, it is the penultimate hop router of the transport tunnel. The bypass tunnel MUST NOT traverse the primary PE or the penultimate link, or share any SRLG with that link.

When a failure hits, the PLR switches all traffic from the transport tunnel to the bypass tunnel and leaves the PW label intact. That keeps the PLR from needing per-PW state, and bypass tunnels can be shared between PWs. The protector MUST already know the PW label assigned by the primary PE (an upstream-assigned label) and MUST look it up in a dedicated label space for that primary PE.

The mechanism assumes IP/MPLS transport tunnels and works with single paths and equal-cost multipaths. With ECMP, if the router cannot reliably detect an egress node failure, it SHOULD treat failure of the direct link as an egress node failure.
sections.eli5: A helper stands just before the broken bridge with a ready-made detour. When the bridge fails, the helper sends everything down the detour without opening any boxes.

sections.title: Context Identifiers and Protector Models
sections.content:
A context identifier is an IPv4 or IPv6 address assigned to each ordered pair of {primary PE, protector}. It must be globally unique or unique in the network's address space. It has two meanings. The ingress PE sets up the transport tunnel to the context identifier instead of the primary PE's own address, so the tunnel reaches the primary PE while also telling the PLR who the protector is. And it names the label space on the protector that holds the PW labels from that primary PE.

The ingress PE learns the context identifier from the primary PE through the Interface_ID TLV in the LDP Label Mapping message. A given PW MUST belong to exactly one {primary PE, protector} pair. For the context identifier's FEC, aggregation MUST NOT be applied and every router MUST assign a unique label.

There are two ways to advertise a context identifier in the IGP. In the first, the primary PE and the protector both advertise it as an address reachable via both, for example as a virtual proxy node, with no IGP extension. In the second, the protector advertises it with an explicit context identifier object that the PLR MUST understand, which does need an IGP extension.

There are two protection models. In the co-located protector model the protector is the backup PE or backup S-PE and forwards straight to the CE or the next backup segment. In the centralized protector model the protector is a dedicated P or PE router that swaps the primary PW label to the backup PW label and sends the traffic on to the backup PE. The centralized model lets multiple primary PEs share one protector, so the number of context identifiers can be bound to the number of primary PEs.
sections.eli5: A context identifier is like a special code name for 'this main place plus this helper'. Everyone along the way uses the code name, so the helper knows to wait with the right keys.

sections.title: Restoration, Reversion and Forwarding State
sections.content:
Local repair is a stopgap. Afterwards, traffic returns to a fully working path in one of three ways. In global repair, a multihomed CE (or an ingress PE hosting a backup PW) moves traffic to the backup PW, triggered for example by PW status notification, VCCV or BFD. In control-plane convergence, if only the link to the primary PE failed, the tunnel can be rerouted around it. In local reversion, the PLR MAY move traffic back to the primary once the failure is resolved; this is optional, MAY be dampened if resources are flapping, and MAY be disabled by configuration.

The RFC recommends using the mechanism together with global repair. If the ingress PE or protector loses contact with the egress PE or S-PE for long, the LDP session may go down, the ingress may bring the primary PW down, or the protector may remove the primary PW label's forwarding entry. So control-plane state may eventually expire if the failure persists.

The RFC includes worked examples of forwarding state. In one, PE2 assigned PW1 the label 100, and on the protector PE4 label 999 points to PE2's label space, where label 100 means pop and send to CE2. On the PLR P3, label 1000 has a primary next hop of pop to PE2 and a backup next hop of swap 2000 toward PE4.
sections.eli5: The detour is only meant to be used for a short while. After that, the delivery company should switch to a proper new route, and optionally switch back when the bridge is fixed.

sections.title: LDP Extensions
sections.content:
A targeted LDP session MUST exist between each primary PE and its protector. In the centralized model, one MUST also exist between each backup PE and the protector. The RFC adds two TLVs.

The Egress Protection Capability TLV (code point 0x0974) is a Capability Parameter TLV (RFC 5561). The protector sends it in its Initialization and Capability messages and it carries one or more context identifiers. Its U-bit MUST be 1 and its F-bit MUST be 0. The S-bit says whether the capability is being advertised (1) or withdrawn (0). A router MUST NOT send PW information to the protector until it has received this TLV.

The Protection FEC Element TLV (type 0x83) identifies a primary PW. It has an Encoding Type field of 1 to 4 for PWid or Generalized PWid with IPv4 or IPv6 PE addresses, a length and variable PW information. The primary PE sends the protector a Label Mapping message with this TLV, an Upstream-Assigned Label TLV carrying the PW label, and an Interface_ID TLV carrying the context identifier. In the centralized model, the backup PE sends a Label Mapping message with an identical Protection FEC Element and a Generic Label TLV, without a context identifier. The protector tells the two apart by whether the context identifier is present, and silently discards a message with an unknown context identifier.
sections.eli5: Before anything breaks, the main place and the helper talk, so the helper writes down every label in advance. Special message types make sure both sides understand each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC argues the mechanism introduces no new security threat. Rerouting traffic via PLRs, protectors and backup PEs is planned and anticipated, and backup PEs can host PWs and LDP sessions anyway. The targeted LDP sessions between primary PE and protector, and between backup PE and protector, are not seen as a new threat.

The general security frameworks still apply: RFC 5920 for MPLS and GMPLS networks, RFC 3209 for RSVP LSPs, RFC 5036 for base LDP and RFC 5561 for LDP capabilities.
sections.eli5: The detour and the helper were already part of the plan, so they do not open new doors for trouble. The usual rules for these networks still apply.
